clusters.name: Your stepfather moving in and your father's separation, 1987
clusters.reason: Around 1987, when you were fourteen: your stepfather Desmond arrived in your life around the time your father and Bettina split over starting a family, and you felt the distance from Desmond while staying warm toward your dad. You made the city chess squad that autumn, out of your depth and grinding hard, which raised your anxiety. These shifts pile up in the same months when your household was shifting.

clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death and your path through the conservatory, 1989–1994
clusters.reason: Around 1989 to 1994: your grandfather Gordon died in 1991 after years of illness, and in the months around his death and after, your household shifted when you all moved into the rebuilt house on Hollin Road with Desmond's children, loud and cramped. You started liking late nights that autumn; you dropped chess and debate, absorbed in music. Your mother filled in your college forms and you chose Wexley because Rafe was there, then fused hard with him as roommates. A wrist injury stopped your playing in the first term, your anxiety rose and your functioning fell; you and Rafe clashed and he moved out. You were lost and low, unable to get going, with your grandfather gone and your mother about to remarry. You holed up high, fixing radios, then drifted through a bleak year at community college. An exchange to Portugal snapped you out of it in early 1994, and you tore through the rest of your degree. Your grandmother Winifred was treated for a thyroid tumour within a year or so of your grandfather's death. These events pile up close together across five years, each person's trouble near another's.

clusters.name: Your relationship with Joelle and the height of your performing, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: Around 1998 to 1999: you bonded with Joelle in early 1998, and by 1999 you were playing the best you ever had, winning competitions. At the same time, insomnia began getting in the way—sleepless nights before concerts though you practised hard. You split with Joelle that summer, and you started with a therapist after the split. One shift alone is a reaction; the height of your performing and the insomnia sit beside your relationship and its end, and the pile of these events in the same months is what holds them together.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's bowel cancer and your move away from Thornbury, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around 2001 to 2004: your grandmother Winifred was found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002, the same time you were running out of steam for performing, less content by the month, your anxiety up and functioning down. You had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in your home town and were done with performing, casting about for what came next. You were on poor terms with your family and friends, and you left Thornbury for Gull Harbour that autumn. You met Marisol at a winter party in early 2003 and left Gull Harbour to live with her in Fenwick by mid-year. You split from her within the year, sank into a deep depression once you were back in Thornbury that winter, and could hardly move from the sofa. You could not face your family—your parents seemed a world away. You relied on friends, and your anxiety was up around them. Your father and your friend Corbin spoke several times during your stay. By January 2004 you had begun swimming laps and requested help from your parents with therapy costs; you returned to your therapist Victor and the gradual recovery started there. Your grandmother died of the bowel cancer in February 2004. These shifts and events cluster around the change in your grandmother's health and your own collapse and recovery, reaching across nearly three years with no settling between them until you reconnected with your therapist and your functioning began to rise.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death and the cutoff from your mother, 2008
clusters.reason: Around 2008: your grandmother Lorna died in January, and your grandfather Clifford died that year or near it. That summer before nursing school you spent four weeks building with Silas at Alder Creek, and you were too drained for conversation—you could barely manage a phone call with your mother. She pressed to visit you, her anxiety up, and you kept the door shut on her; the visit went wrong and she never got inside. You left for nursing school in Marlow Sound that September and stopped speaking to your mother when you moved; the silence held for roughly a year. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke that January with months of rehabilitation ahead. These events pile up around the losses of your grandparents and your own withdrawal from your mother into nursing school, each person's trouble near another's in the months around those changes.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren and the stress in her family, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around 2017 to 2019: you married Wren in March 2017, and you saw your mother a bit less once she came along. That October 2019, a street party and a fundraising dinner and the drive to the lake for her mother Frances's retirement party swamped Wren—her symptom and anxiety up, functioning down. Wren's family talks all day; nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. You were too strict laying out a plan to settle her when she was swamped, your anxiety up and you overfunctioning. She settled once the weekend had a plan, but you awoke from the small hours at the lake weekend with no more sleep, your symptom and anxiety up, and you could only pull back as the others rose. You felt you didn't belong. Wren's anxiety rose when you'd had no sleep at family occasions. These events cluster around your marriage and the intensifying stress of proximity to Wren's close-knit family, piling up across the weeks of that autumn visit when the competing demands on Wren and the sleeplessness it triggered in you showed the strain of the fusion within her family and your own distance from it.

periods.name: the year I left home
periods.words: The first is the year I left home: I went off to the conservatory, hurt my wrist in the first term and couldn't play, dropped out and drifted at my mother's place, then spent a bleak spell at the community college shooting pool every night until an exchange in Portugal snapped me out of it and I tore through the rest of my coursework.

periods.name: the long slump
periods.words: The second is the long slump, roughly ages 27 to 29, when nothing at home felt right, I moved to Gull Harbour away from nearly everyone I knew, then followed Marisol to Fenwick, and when that fell apart I went under, a depression I only really climbed out of after nursing school.
